issues.description: Log buffering complects identity, time, and lifecycle across three files with no single owner of the buffer's state
issues.detail: The early buffer is created in _start_log_buffering, optionally promoted in _on_cleanup, flushed in init_recording, and silently dropped in three other paths. Five entry points all mutate the same _early_log_handler reference. This is COMPLECTED: lifecycle state, replay decision, and OTLP discovery are intertwined. A small value-oriented buffer object owning its own start/stop/replay would decompose this.

issues.description: _flush_early_log_buffer reaches into the root logger to find an OTLP handler by isinstance — place-oriented coupling
issues.detail: The replay path scans logging.getLogger().handlers looking for a LoggingHandler instance installed as a side effect of _setup_cloud_tracer. That is identity-by-position: the buffer's replay target is whatever happens to be attached to the root logger right now. INCIDENTAL-COMPLEXITY. _setup_cloud_tracer should return the handler (a value) and the buffer should replay into it directly.

issues.description: _BufferingHandler has unbounded buffer with no max size or time bound
issues.detail: buffer: list[LogRecord] grows for the entire pre-session window with no cap. A crash that takes minutes to surface, or a chatty dependency, can balloon memory. The essential complication is 'keep recent records until we know whether to replay'; an unbounded list is incidental. A bounded deque with a documented limit makes the time semantics explicit.

issues.description: _shutdown_telemetry removes all LoggingHandler instances from root, not just the one it installed
issues.detail: The loop strips every LoggingHandler subclass from the root logger before force_flush. If a user attached their own OTLP LoggingHandler for their own pipeline, it gets silently detached. The provider doesn't own those handlers. Track the specific handler instance installed by _setup_cloud_tracer and remove only that one — identity matters here.

issues.description: Unrelated changes mixed into a crash-logs PR — worker ordering, makefile -n auto removal, test skip
issues.detail: The reorder of _pending_assignments before _queue_msg, the removal of pytest-xdist parallelism, and the dropped test_plugin_google_stt.py are real changes with their own rationale and risk, unrelated to log buffering. Bundling them complects review: a reviewer cannot accept the crash-log fix without also accepting a serial test run. Separate commits or PRs.

issues.description: Bare 'except Exception' in _on_cleanup swallows the reason crash-log upload failed
issues.detail: init_recording on the cleanup path is wrapped in except Exception with logger.exception, then _stop_log_buffering. The buffered records — the actual crash evidence — are dropped on the floor with no fallback emission to the local logger. The whole point of this PR is troubleshooting; losing the buffer when the upload path fails defeats the goal. Consider replaying to stderr as a fallback.

review.summary: The intent — capture pre-session crash logs — is essential and worth solving. The implementation is EASY-NOT-SIMPLE: a single buffer's identity is mutated across five methods in two files, its replay target is discovered by isinstance scan of the root logger, and lifecycle decisions are scattered. The hammock question that should have been asked first: 'what is the value here, and who owns its time semantics?' A small buffer object that owns start/stop/replay, plus _setup_cloud_tracer returning its handler as a value, would decompose the whole thing. Also: unrelated changes (worker ordering, removed test parallelism, skipped test) are complecting the review itself.
